prompt: In a push-based pipeline, what holds a credential that can change the cluster?

choices.text: Only the developer who merged the change
choices.why: The merge needs no cluster credential at all; the job that runs after it does.

choices.text: The CI system that runs the deploy job
choices.why: Right. To push into the cluster, the job needs a key to it, and so does everything else that runs in that CI.

choices.text: Nobody, because the registry applies the image
choices.why: A registry stores images. It never changes a cluster.

choices.text: An agent that runs inside the cluster
choices.why: That is the pull arrangement, where the key never leaves the cluster.

prompt: An hour after a push deploy, somebody scales a deployment by hand. In a push setup, when is that noticed?

choices.text: Only if a later deploy overwrites it
choices.why: Right. The pipeline acted once and is gone; nothing looks again until the next run.

choices.text: Within one interval, because the pipeline keeps checking
choices.why: A push pipeline runs once per change. Checking on an interval is what a reconciler does.

choices.text: Immediately, because kubectl refuses manual changes
choices.why: kubectl accepts a manual scale like any other change.

choices.text: At the end of the CI job that deployed it
choices.why: That job finished an hour before the change.

prompt: Which of these are costs of the pull arrangement, as the lesson lists them? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Whoever can write to the repository can change production
choices.why: Right. The repository becomes the thing to guard.

choices.text: The agent has to be installed, upgraded and watched
choices.why: Right. It is one more program running in the cluster.

choices.text: The CI system needs a stronger cluster credential
choices.why: The reverse: in pull, the CI system needs none.

choices.text: A change takes effect when the agent next looks
choices.why: Right. The delay is the interval, or the time to notice a change.

prompt: Put the four OpenGitOps principles in the order the lesson lists them.
trap: Describing the state comes first, keeping it second, fetching it third, and the loop that never stops last.

prompt: Match each principle to what it forbids.

pairs.right: A deploy that is a list of commands
A tag that means something else tomorrow
A pipeline outside holding the cluster's keys
A manual change that lasts until noticed

right_distractors: A cluster with more than one namespace

prompt: Does a system that stores its desired state in a versioned OCI registry, not in Git, meet the principles?

choices.text: Yes, but only if the registry also runs CI
choices.why: Running CI has nothing to do with where the state is kept.

choices.text: No: the second principle names Git explicitly
choices.why: It says versioned and immutable. Git is not in any of the four.

choices.text: Yes: it asks for versioned, not for Git
choices.why: Right. Git is the common choice, not a requirement, and Flux can read desired state from an OCI registry.

choices.text: No, because only Git can be pulled by an agent
choices.why: An agent can pull from a registry or a bucket as well.

prompt: Why did the GitOps tooling grow around Kubernetes rather than some other platform?

choices.text: Its controllers already reconcile; GitOps extends the loop
choices.why: Right. A Deployment compares replicas wanted with replicas running; GitOps moves the 'wanted' one step outwards.

choices.text: Kubernetes has a Git server built into its API
choices.why: It has no Git server; the agents read Git from outside.

choices.text: Only Kubernetes lets an agent run inside the cluster it manages
choices.why: Agents run on any platform; what Kubernetes offers is a declarative API driven by loops.

choices.text: The principles require Kubernetes manifests
choices.why: The principles name no platform at all.

prompt: A Git commit is identified by a ___ computed from its content and its parents, so it names one tree of files for ever.
Which path does the lesson recommend for the lab?

choices.text: Docker Desktop on Windows or macOS
choices.why: It runs kind, but container names on Docker's network are not reachable from your terminal there.

choices.text: A cluster shared by the course's students
choices.why: The course provides no cluster; you build your own.

choices.text: An Ubuntu VM made with Multipass
choices.why: Right. Everything is written for Linux, and the VM behaves the same on every host.

choices.text: A cloud VM rented by the hour
choices.why: It works and costs money for every hour; it is named, not recommended.

prompt: How many GiB of memory does the lesson ask the Multipass VM for?
sha256sum --check prints FAILED for the kind binary you downloaded. What does the lesson tell you to do?

choices.text: Edit the checksum file to match the download
choices.why: That makes the check agree with whatever arrived, which defeats it.

choices.text: Delete it and download it again
choices.why: Right. A failed check means the file is not the one the project published; never install it anyway.

choices.text: Install it anyway, since the version number matched
choices.why: The version in the name says nothing about the bytes you received.

choices.text: Run it with sudo so the check is skipped
choices.why: sudo changes who runs a program, not whether it is the right program.

prompt: Why does the node need a hosts.toml saying that localhost:5001 is http://registry:5000?

choices.text: Because the registry refuses connections from localhost
choices.why: It accepts them; your own push used localhost:5001.

choices.text: To make the registry reachable from your own terminal
choices.why: Your terminal already reaches it through the published port.

choices.text: In the node, localhost is the node
choices.why: Right. The same name means two places, and the file tells containerd which one is meant.

choices.text: Because containerd cannot pull images without TLS
choices.why: The file says http on purpose, and containerd accepts it for that host.

prompt: What do the two extraPortMappings in cluster.yaml give you?

choices.text: curl localhost:8080 and 8081 reach the cluster's ports 30080 and 30081
choices.why: Right. Each maps a port on your machine to a port on the node, so no port-forward is needed.

choices.text: Two extra nodes, one for staging and one for production
choices.why: Nodes are listed under nodes; the file has one.

choices.text: Access to the Kubernetes API from other computers
choices.why: The API is reached through the kubeconfig, and listenAddress keeps these ports local anyway.

choices.text: A second registry on port 8081
choices.why: The registry is a container of its own on 5001.

prompt: Where does bulletin's version number come from?

choices.text: The Git commit that deployed it
choices.why: Nothing in the image knows which commit deployed it.

choices.text: A build argument baked into the image
choices.why: Right. bulletin:1.0 says 1.0 wherever it runs.

choices.text: The MESSAGE variable in the manifest
choices.why: MESSAGE is the second line, the message.

choices.text: A file in /secrets read on every request
choices.why: That is where the token comes from.

prompt: Why does index.cgi print the first twelve characters of the token's SHA-256 instead of the token?

choices.text: SHA-256 decrypts the token for display
choices.why: A hash cannot be reversed, which is exactly why it is safe to show.

choices.text: It tells two tokens apart without revealing either
choices.why: Right. The fingerprint changes when the token does, and is useless to whoever reads the page.

choices.text: The token is too long to fit on one line
choices.why: Length has nothing to do with it; a secret is never printed.

choices.text: httpd refuses to send text from /secrets
choices.why: httpd sends whatever the script prints.

prompt: A file mounted at /secrets/token is replaced while the pod runs. When does bulletin's page show the new fingerprint?

choices.text: When a new image is built
choices.why: The token is not in the image.

choices.text: Never, because httpd caches the page
choices.why: There is no index.html to cache; the script produces each answer.

choices.text: When the pod is restarted
choices.why: That would be true of a program that read the file once at start; this one reads it per request.

choices.text: On the next request
choices.why: Right. A CGI script runs again for every request and reads the file each time.

prompt: What does staging/bulletin.yaml describe?

choices.text: What is running in the cluster right now
choices.why: It is the wish, and the cluster may differ from it.

choices.text: The commands that create staging, in order
choices.why: It contains no commands; the order is only the order the objects must exist in.

choices.text: What should be true in the cluster
choices.why: Right. It names objects and their fields, and says nothing about how to get there.

choices.text: How to build the bulletin image
choices.why: That is the Dockerfile, in the other repository.

prompt: What is ~/fleet.git, made with git init --bare, standing in for?

choices.text: The Git server that lesson 2 sets up
choices.why: Right. A bare repository has no working files, which is what a server keeps.

choices.text: A backup of the cluster's objects
choices.why: It holds the description, not anything read from the cluster.

choices.text: The image registry
choices.why: The registry holds images; the repository holds manifests.

choices.text: A second copy of ~/fleet to edit in
choices.why: You edit in ~/fleet; the bare repository has no files to edit.

prompt: The first object in staging/bulletin.yaml is the ___, because the other two live inside it.
You edit staging/bulletin.yaml in ~/fleet and save it, without committing. What does reconcile.sh do?

choices.text: It refuses to run until the file is committed
choices.why: It keeps running and applies what was last pushed.

choices.text: It applies your saved file on the next pass
choices.why: It never reads ~/fleet; it reads ~/.reconcile, pulled from the remote.

choices.text: It commits the change for you
choices.why: It only pulls; it never writes to the repository.

choices.text: Nothing until you push
choices.why: Right. What is on your disk and not in the repository does not exist for it.

prompt: How many seconds does reconcile.sh wait between passes?
After the push, the loop printed deployment.apps/bulletin configured. Why did that start a rollout?

choices.text: The pod template changed, and a new template means new pods
choices.why: Right. MESSAGE is in the template, so changing it replaces the pods.

choices.text: The loop deletes and recreates the deployment
choices.why: It applies; Kubernetes compares and patches.

choices.text: The image tag changed from 1.0 to 1.1
choices.why: The image stayed 1.0; only the message changed.

choices.text: Every apply restarts the pods it touches
choices.why: An apply that changes nothing leaves the pods alone, which is why most passes print nothing.

prompt: What does the lesson call drift?

choices.text: A change to the cluster nobody committed
choices.why: Right. A manual scale, an edit to test something, a deletion by mistake.

choices.text: The delay between a push and the next pass of the loop
choices.why: That is the interval, which is expected.

choices.text: A new version of an image in the registry
choices.why: A new image changes nothing until a manifest names it.

choices.text: A commit that has not been pushed yet
choices.why: That is a local change; the cluster is not involved.

prompt: During an incident you run kubectl scale --replicas=5 while the reconciler runs. What happens?

choices.text: It is back to the file's 2 within one interval
choices.why: Right. The next apply puts the field back; the way to change it quickly is a quick commit.

choices.text: It stays at 5 until somebody edits the file
choices.why: The loop applies the file on every pass, so 5 lasts one interval at most.

choices.text: Git records the scale as a new commit
choices.why: Nothing writes the cluster's state back into Git.

choices.text: The reconciler stops, because the cluster changed
choices.why: It does not watch for changes at all; it applies on a timer.

prompt: You delete the Service from the file and push. Why does kubectl get service still list it?

choices.text: The loop has not passed yet
choices.why: The prune block waited past a pass, and the loop had already applied the shorter file.

choices.text: kubectl apply -f only knows the objects in the files it is given
choices.why: Right. Nothing records what was applied before, so nothing deletes what disappeared. That is pruning.

choices.text: The commit was rejected by the bare repository
choices.why: The push succeeded, and the loop reported the new commit.

choices.text: Services cannot be deleted while pods use them
choices.why: They can; nothing asked for it.

prompt: Which limits of the shell reconciler does the lesson name? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: It cannot apply a Deployment
choices.why: It applied one on every pass.

choices.text: Its state is a line of output on one machine
choices.why: Right. The real tools keep it as objects anybody can query.

choices.text: It never deletes objects removed from Git
choices.why: Right. That is pruning, which lesson 3 turns on.

choices.text: It runs with credentials for the whole cluster
choices.why: Right. Lesson 11 narrows them.

prompt: Right after installing Docker, docker ps says permission denied on /var/run/docker.sock. What fixes it?

choices.text: Logging out and back in
choices.why: Right. Group membership is read at login, and the install added you to the docker group.

choices.text: Reinstalling Docker
choices.why: The installation worked; the terminal just predates your new group.

choices.text: Running every command with sudo from now on
choices.why: It works and leaves root-owned files in your home directory.

choices.text: Deleting /var/run/docker.sock
choices.why: That removes the daemon's socket and breaks Docker for everyone.

prompt: Match each message to its cause.

pairs.right: The node does not know where localhost:5001 is

pairs.left: node(s) already exist for a cluster

prompt: The pods are Running, but curl localhost:8080 says Connection refused. The cluster was made from a file without extraPortMappings. What fixes it?

choices.text: Change the Service to type LoadBalancer
choices.why: Nothing on your machine would lead to it either.

choices.text: Delete it and recreate it from this lesson's YAML
choices.why: Right. Port mappings are fixed when the node container is created.

choices.text: Add the mappings to the file and run kubectl apply
choices.why: cluster.yaml is read by kind at creation, not by the cluster.

choices.text: Restart the registry container
choices.why: The registry is not in the path between curl and the pods.

prompt: A team keeps every manifest in Git and deploys by running kubectl apply from a CI job. Is it GitOps?

choices.text: Yes, because the manifests are versioned in Git
choices.why: Versioned is one principle of four.

choices.text: Yes, as long as the CI job runs on every merge
choices.why: That is continuous deployment, which is a different question.

choices.text: No: nothing pulls the state or keeps reconciling it
choices.why: Right. The third and fourth principles are missing.

choices.text: No, because GitOps forbids CI pipelines
choices.why: GitOps keeps CI for building and testing; it only takes the cluster away from it.

prompt: How can a team that releases once a week still use GitOps?

choices.text: With a weekly merge to production
choices.why: Right. GitOps is how a change reaches the cluster; when it is merged is a separate decision.

choices.text: By keeping production manifests outside Git
choices.why: Then production would not be reconciled at all.

choices.text: By pausing the agent for six days out of seven
choices.why: A paused agent stops correcting drift too.

choices.text: It cannot: GitOps deploys every commit at once
choices.why: Only what is merged into the path the agent reads gets deployed.

prompt: A broken manifest is merged. What does GitOps change about what happens next?

choices.text: The break is a commit, and its revert is applied by the same loop
choices.why: Right. It does not stop the break; it makes the way back an ordinary commit.

choices.text: The agent refuses to apply a manifest that would break the service
choices.why: An agent applies a broken manifest as faithfully as a good one.

choices.text: Nothing, because the cluster ignores manifests it cannot parse
choices.why: A manifest that parses can still describe something broken.

choices.text: The CI system rolls the cluster back on its own
choices.why: In GitOps the CI system has no access to the cluster.

prompt: Production is failing and the fix is to raise replicas from 2 to 6. A reconciler applies the repository every 3 minutes. What is the fastest change that lasts?

choices.text: kubectl scale, then a commit next week
choices.why: The scale lasts until the next pass, at most three minutes.

choices.text: A one-line commit to the replicas field, merged and pushed
choices.why: Right. A manual scale would be undone within three minutes; the commit is what the loop keeps.

choices.text: kubectl scale, followed by stopping the reconciler for good
choices.why: That trades one incident for a cluster nobody reconciles.

choices.text: Editing the pods directly with kubectl edit
choices.why: Pods belong to the deployment, which replaces them, and the loop resets the deployment.

prompt: Order what happens when the message changes, from your editor to the new page.
items: You push it to the remote
The loop pulls the new commit
kubectl apply reports the deployment configured
New pods start with the new message
trap: Nothing reaches the cluster before it reaches the remote, and nothing reaches the remote before the commit.

prompt: CI builds bulletin 1.1 and pushes it to the registry, and nobody touches the fleet repository. What runs in staging?

choices.text: 1.1, on the reconciler's next pass
choices.why: The reconciler reads the repository, not the registry.

choices.text: 1.1, as soon as the push finishes
choices.why: A push to a registry changes no cluster.

choices.text: Still 1.0
choices.why: Right. The registry holds the image, but the desired state still names 1.0, and only that is applied.

choices.text: Neither, because the tags now conflict
choices.why: Two tags of one image coexist without conflict.

prompt: A push pipeline's apply step fails halfway. What state is the cluster in?

choices.text: Locked until the pipeline turns green
choices.why: Nothing locks the cluster.

choices.text: Half changed, until somebody runs it again
choices.why: Right. The job is gone and nothing finishes the change.

choices.text: Rolled back to the last good deploy
choices.why: A pipeline does not roll back by itself.

choices.text: Exactly as before the run
choices.why: Whatever applied before the failure stays applied.

prompt: Which costs does pull bring, as the lesson lists them? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The CI system needs a credential into the cluster
choices.why: That is push's problem, which pull removes.

choices.text: The agent must be installed, upgraded and watched
choices.why: Right. It is software you run.

choices.text: Whoever can write to the repository can change production
choices.why: Right. Lesson 2 guards it.

choices.text: A change waits for the agent's next look
choices.why: Right. Not when the pipeline finishes.

prompt: Which of these satisfies the principle 'versioned and immutable' without Git?

choices.text: An OCI registry holding manifests
choices.why: Right. Flux reads desired state from one in lesson 7.

choices.text: The cluster's own database
choices.why: It holds the current state, not its history.

choices.text: A wiki page with the manifests pasted in
choices.why: A page can be edited without a fixed version.

choices.text: A shared folder people edit in place
choices.why: Nothing keeps the old versions.

prompt: Why did the GitOps tooling grow on Kubernetes, though the principles never name it?

choices.text: Its controllers already reconcile
choices.why: Right. A Deployment compares wanted with running.

choices.text: The CNCF requires Kubernetes for GitOps
choices.why: The principles are about any system.

choices.text: Kubernetes stores every past state
choices.why: It keeps the current state only.

choices.text: Only Kubernetes can read Git
choices.why: Git is read by the agent, not the platform.

prompt: Why does the course recommend an Ubuntu virtual machine over Docker Desktop?

choices.text: The VM is faster than any laptop
choices.why: Speed is not the reason.

choices.text: Some commands reach containers by name from your terminal
choices.why: Right. Docker Desktop does not route those names.

choices.text: Multipass includes Kubernetes
choices.why: It makes a VM; kind makes the cluster.

choices.text: Docker Desktop cannot run kind
choices.why: It runs kind; most of the course works.

prompt: sha256sum --check prints FAILED for a downloaded kubectl. What should you do?

choices.text: Edit the checksum file to match
choices.why: That defeats the check.

choices.text: Install it with sudo
choices.why: sudo changes nothing about a corrupt file.

choices.text: Run it once to see if it works
choices.why: A damaged or replaced binary may still run.

choices.text: Delete it and download again
choices.why: Right. Never install a file that failed the check.

prompt: Why does the node need hosts.toml to pull localhost:5001/bulletin:1.0?

choices.text: containerd cannot read tags without it
choices.why: Tags are read the same way either way.

choices.text: Inside the node, localhost is the node itself
choices.why: Right. The file sends it to the registry container.

choices.text: The registry refuses requests without it
choices.why: The registry accepts any client.

choices.text: kind blocks port 5001 by default
choices.why: Nothing blocks it; nothing listens there.

prompt: Where does each bulletin image get its version from?

choices.text: A build argument baked into the image
choices.why: Right. bulletin:1.0 says 1.0 wherever it runs.

choices.text: The Git commit of the fleet repository
choices.why: fleet describes where it runs, not what it is.

choices.text: An environment variable set by the manifest
choices.why: The message comes from there, not the version.

choices.text: The tag the registry stores it under
choices.why: The tag is a name; the version is inside.

prompt: What does git init --bare make, and why use one here?

choices.text: A repository that cannot be pushed to
choices.why: It is exactly what you push to.

choices.text: A repository with no working files, standing in for a server
choices.why: Right. Lesson 2 replaces it with Gitea.

choices.text: A copy of ~/fleet that updates itself
choices.why: It changes only when something pushes.

choices.text: A repository without history
choices.why: It keeps the full history.

prompt: You edit staging/bulletin.yaml but do not push. What does the loop apply?

choices.text: Your edited file
choices.why: Your working files are not in its clone.

choices.text: A merge of both versions
choices.why: It never merges.

choices.text: Nothing until you push twice
choices.why: One push is enough.

choices.text: The last pushed version
choices.why: Right. It reads only what was pushed.

prompt: How many seconds does the course's reconcile.sh wait between passes?
During an incident somebody scales production with kubectl. What is the GitOps way to make it last?

choices.text: Annotate the deployment as manual
choices.why: The loop does not read annotations.

choices.text: Stop the reconciler for good
choices.why: Then nothing keeps the cluster in sync.

choices.text: A quick commit with the new count
choices.why: Right. The loop would undo anything else.

choices.text: Scale again after each reconciliation
choices.why: The loop wins every round.

choices.text: docker images

choices.text: No: GitOps is how changes arrive, not when
choices.why: Right. They merge into production weekly.
